claude.sample_unit: deliveries (2019 AMC 8007; 2020 AMC 9623; clinical research network 37673)
models_evaluated: Logistic regression with L2 regularization PPD risk model (baseline)
Fairness through blindness (race nullified)
Retrained without race
Reweighing variants

links.outcome: Fairness metrics by race subgroup (White vs non-White) across three datasets before deployment
links.effect: Baseline model met equal-error-rate metrics but failed statistical parity and disparate impact in AMC data; clinical research network metrics were all within range, so fairness varied across datasets.
links.quote: The clinical research network dataset’s observed metrics are all within the defined fairness range.

links.outcome: Effect of five debiasing approaches on fairness metrics and model accuracy
links.effect: All approaches largely improved fairness metrics except predictive parity difference; approaches 2, 4, 5 most successful; blindness improved fairness without compromising performance; reweighing reduced sensitivity by about 0.25.
links.quote: While it is commonly a concern that debiasing method may compromise predictive performance, for our study, they improved fairness without compromise.

links.outcome: Governance review of race as model input and effect of removing race on performance and fairness
links.effect: Reviewers questioned race as a predictor; removing race (fairness through blindness) improved statistical parity difference from -0.175, -0.011, -0.122 to -0.094, -0.056, 0.004 without loss of AUC.
links.quote: The review of this model included an examination of race as a predictor in the model from a modeling and end-user perspective, and questioned the use of race for its potential impact on model bias.

links.outcome: Threshold selection using decision curve net benefit, sensitivity, and positive prediction rates
links.effect: Net benefit was highest at 0.3-0.4 thresholds; 0.2 predicted 19-23% positive versus 13-18% at 0.3 and 11-15% at 0.4; threshold 0.3 balanced true and false positives while 0.2 missed fewer at-risk patients.
links.quote: A threshold of 0.3 produces positive predictions that are close to the observed prevalence at the AMC, while a threshold of 0.2 generates more positive predictions potentially allowing us to capture more at-risk patients albeit with false positive predictions.

links.outcome: Model performance on local post-development AMC data (2019, 2020) against reference outcome
links.effect: Model maintained predictive performance on local later-year data (AUC 0.96 in 2019, 0.97 in 2020; sensitivity 0.95, 0.97 at threshold 0.3) though it showed unequal positive prediction rates.
links.quote: We found that the original model maintained predictive performance and, while satisfying fairness metrics that prioritized equal error rates, did not create equal positive prediction rates between White and non-White patients.

links.outcome: Model performance and fairness in a later year (COVID-19) and a different clinical research network population
links.effect: AUC remained high (0.94-0.97) across datasets, but fairness varied: biased on statistical parity in AMC data, generally unbiased in the clinical research network data.
links.quote: The findings revealed that the model exhibited biased performance in the AMC data but showed less bias in the clinical research network data, thus showing fairness metrics may vary across datasets.

links.outcome: Multidisciplinary governance review of model inputs and clinician interpretability changed the deployed model design
links.effect: Expert review raised concern about clinicians interpreting race as a predictor, and this fed into selecting fairness through blindness as the revised model.
links.quote: More importantly, it meets the expert feedback highlighting the difficulties clinicians might face interpreting race as a top predictor in a clinical decision support tool.

unlisted_practices: Decision curve analysis (net benefit) to choose classification threshold
Comparing multiple debiasing approaches (blindness, reweighing) before implementation

models_evaluated: Baseline postpartum depression logistic regression risk model
Approach 1: fairness through blindness/nullified race using original parameters
Approach 2: removed race and retrained logistic regression
Approach 3: reweighing by White/non-White race using observed PPD rate
Approach 4: reweighing using literature PPD prevalence
Approach 5: removed race and retrained with reweighing using literature rate

links.effect: Baseline AUCs were 0.96, 0.97, and 0.94; AMC data showed biased performance, whereas clinical research network data showed less bias.
links.quote: The findings revealed that the model exhibited biased performance in the AMC data but showed less bias in the clinical research network data, thus showing fairness metrics may vary across datasets.

links.effect: At threshold 0.3, baseline statistical parity/disparate impact were −0.175/0.403 (2019 AMC) and −0.122/0.599 (2020 AMC), outside [−0.1, 0.1]/[0.8, 1.25].
links.quote: However, both statistical parity difference and disparate impact did not meet the fairness criteria.

links.outcome: debiasing effects on fairness and accuracy
links.effect: Approach 2 improved statistical parity to −0.094, −0.056, and 0.004 with AUC 0.97, 0.96, 0.95, but AMC disparate impact remained 0.49/0.735.
links.quote: Despite various methods employed to improve fairness metrics and meet the definition of fairness, the efforts achieved a limited reduction in the predicted positivity rate gap, while still maintaining sensitivity.

links.effect: Threshold 0.2 predicted 19% and 23% positive, versus 0.3 at 13% and 18% and 0.4 at 11% and 15%; lower thresholds had higher sensitivity.
links.quote: A risk threshold of 0.3 seems to be most balanced in true positive and false positives, but a threshold of 0.2 will miss fewer at-risk patients.

models_evaluated: logistic regression with L2 regularization

links.outcome: effect of debiasing methods on model fairness and predictive performance
links.effect: Fairness through blindness improved statistical parity difference to acceptable range without compromising AUC (0.95-0.97) or sensitivity (0.94), whereas reweighing approaches decreased sensitivity by around 0.25.
links.quote: While it is commonly a concern that debiasing method may compromise predictive performance, for our study, they improved fairness without compromise.

screen.practice: pre-implementation fairness evaluation, threshold selection, and debiasing
screen.reason: Empirical pre-implementation evaluation comparing specific debiasing strategies (fairness through blindness vs reweighing) and decision-threshold selection methods for equity and clinical appropriateness prior to EHR implementation.
